name: Math Lessons for a Living Education
line: A parent teaches and checks Math Lessons for a Living Education. In AMP, both happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs Math Lessons for a Living Education: daily lessons a parent teaches and checks. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
verdict: Math Lessons for a Living Education is a series of printed workbooks of daily, story-led lessons. A parent teaches each lesson and checks the work [1][5]. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous: every answer is checked and explained, updates the learner's level and sets the next problem.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. Math Lessons for a Living Education places a child with a Readiness Test for each level. The adult reads the result and picks the book [1][4]. After that, the adult checks each lesson's work [1][5].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem in front of them: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Math Lessons for a Living Education the unit is the daily lesson: a short story, copywork, oral narration and a hands-on activity, which the parent reads and guides with the child [1][5]. A meta-analysis of 55 studies found that worked examples improve mathematics performance [11].

reasons.title: Feedback on every answer
reasons.body: After every answer AMP shows whether it was right, the correct answer and the worked steps, before the next problem. In Math Lessons for a Living Education the parent checks the lesson's work after it is done [1][5]. A meta-analysis of 40 studies of computer-based feedback, across mixed ages and subjects, found the largest average effect for feedback that explains [10].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. Math Lessons for a Living Education places review at fixed points in the book: optional review activities, and review lessons that open and close Level 5 [2][3]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later on the researchers' own test, against 38% for practice in blocks [9].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, on one map of skills from counting through precalculus. A learner further along in geometry than in fractions gets work at both levels, and repeated misses send practice back to what a skill builds on. Math Lessons for a Living Education places a child in one level, one book for a grade, and follows its lessons in order [1][2][4]. In the pages we read, no rule for when to move on is given, and the adult decides [1][2][3].

rows.range: Levels 1 to 6, for grades 1 to 6 [1][4]. Principles of Mathematics, a separate series, covers grades 7 and 8 [6].
rows.start: A Readiness Test for each level, as a PDF. The adult reads the result and picks the book [1][4].
rows.teaching: A parent teaches from the book: a short story, copywork, oral narration and hands-on manipulatives [1][2][5]. Optional video lessons [7].
rows.next: The next lesson in the book, in a fixed order on a daily schedule [1][2].
rows.mastery: None found in the pages we read. The adult decides when to move on [1][2][3].
rows.review: Optional review activities, and review lessons at fixed places in the book, such as the start and end of Level 5 [2][3]. The same for every child.
rows.print: Print is the course: full-color, perforated, three-hole-punched workbooks [1][2][4]. The same book for every child at that level.
rows.adult: Reads and teaches each lesson, sets out manipulatives, checks the work and sets the pace, following a daily schedule [1][5].
rows.reports: None built in. The adult keeps records. The Level 6 teacher's guide includes quizzes [4].
rows.evidence: No outcome study is cited on its product pages [1].

theirs: Math Lessons for a Living Education is a math series from Master Books, a Christian homeschool imprint of New Leaf Publishing Group [1][8]. Angela O'Dell wrote it [1]. Levels 1 to 6 cover grades 1 to 6, and Principles of Mathematics, a separate series by a different author, covers grades 7 and 8 [1][4][6]. A Christian worldview is a stated aim of the books [5][6].

A Readiness Test for each level helps the adult pick a book [1][4]. Each level is a full-color workbook of short lessons laid out on a daily schedule [1][2]. A lesson weaves together a short story, copywork, oral narration and a hands-on activity, with manipulatives to cut out [1][4]. The parent reads the lesson with the child, guides the activity and checks the work [1][5]. Optional video lessons are offered through Master Books Academy [7].
credit: Hands-on learning: physical manipulatives, copywork, oral narration and a story running through the lessons [1][2][5].
A parent teaches each lesson in person, from a daily schedule laid out in the book [1][5].
Review lessons are built into the books [2][3].

theirs: We found no outcome study of Math Lessons for a Living Education on its product pages [1].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. In a meta-analysis of 40 studies of computer-based feedback, across mixed ages and subjects, feedback that explains had the largest average effect, 0.49, against 0.32 for the correct answer alone and 0.05 for right or wrong only [10]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% against 38% for practice in blocks a month later, on the researchers' own test [9]. AMP shows the correct answer and the worked steps after every answer, and brings learned skills back mixed with other math.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: You want to teach math yourself from a book, with stories, copywork and hands-on manipulatives.
amp: You want each answer checked and explained the moment it is given, with no pages to grade.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice, mixed with other math.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math.
You want one program from counting through precalculus.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Math Lessons for a Living Education?
questions.answer: Math Lessons for a Living Education is daily lessons a parent teaches from a workbook and checks [1][5]. AMP has no separate test: every answer is checked, explained and sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Math Lessons for a Living Education work?
questions.answer: We found no outcome study of it on its product pages [1].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. A learner can keep the book for its stories and hands-on lessons and practice in AMP too. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
